strengths: Addresses an underexplored and important problem: reliable open-ended multilingual medical reasoning, including several low-resource African/South Asian languages (Amharic, Yoruba, Hausa, Swahili, Hindi, Bengali).

Introduces a new open-ended benchmark (CUREMED-BENCH) with single verifiable answers and explicit reasoning traces across 13 languages, contrasting with mostly multiple-choice/monolingual prior benchmarks; dataset construction includes native-speaker and medical-expert verification with reported quality scores.

Comprehensive experimental scope: comparisons against 28 baseline models across multiple parameter scales (1.5B-72B), systematic ablations isolating the contribution of code-switched SFT vs. naive SFT and curriculum GRPO vs. naive RFT, and out-of-distribution evaluation on three external benchmarks (MMedBench, MedExpQA, MedQA).
Detailed reproducibility appendix documenting prompts, reward weighting, verifier prompts, and training hyperparameters, which aids methodological transparency.

Consistent and large empirical gains in both logical correctness and language consistency across scales and languages, with clear scaling trends and reduced performance disparity between high- and low-resource languages.
weaknesses: Heavy, largely unmitigated dependence on GPT-4o/GPT-4.1 across nearly the entire pipeline (question generation, filtering, open-ended conversion, correctness reward scoring, and evaluation judging), raising concerns about circularity and reward/evaluation biases that are only partially addressed by using different judge models for training vs. eval.

Despite claims of 'extensive automatic and human evaluations' of the trained models' outputs, only the benchmark construction (not the model outputs at evaluation time) underwent human verification; the actual RQ1-RQ4 results rely solely on an LLM-as-judge pipeline, so the central performance claims are not independently human-validated, weakening the soundness of the comparative results.
The 'closed-source multilingual reward model that performs competitively on RewardBench' used during RL training is not identified, limiting reproducibility of a core training component.

Comparisons between CURE-MED (trained/fine-tuned in-domain on the benchmark's train split) and 28 zero-shot baselines are somewhat asymmetric; while OOD results partially address this, the primary results largely reflect in-distribution advantage rather than a fully controlled comparison.

Language-consistency judgments (both as an RL reward and as an evaluation metric) rely on GPT-4.1/GPT-4o language identification, which may itself be unreliable for the lowest-resource languages studied (e.g., Yoruba, Hausa, Amharic), potentially undermining the validity of exactly the results the paper emphasizes most.

Dataset size (15,774 examples across 13 languages) yields modest per-language test partitions once split 80/20 and further divided by language, raising questions about the statistical robustness of fine-grained per-language findings despite reported standard deviations.

Methodological novelty is moderate: the framework largely composes existing techniques (code-switched CoT SFT, GRPO, curriculum learning by resource tier) rather than introducing fundamentally new algorithms.

Human verification details for the dataset (number of annotators per language, inter-annotator agreement, consent procedures) are underspecified beyond aggregate 1-5 ratings, limiting assessment of annotation reliability.

strengths: Addresses an under-explored and practically important gap: multilingual, open-ended medical reasoning evaluation and training, including several genuinely low-resource languages (Amharic, Yoruba, Hausa, Swahili).

Extensive experimental scope: 28 baselines across model families and scales, per-language breakdowns, OOD transfer to three external benchmarks (MMedBench, MedExpQA, MedQA), and a battery of ablations (code-switched SFT vs. naive SFT, curriculum RL vs. naive RFT, curriculum ordering, additional recent baselines like Qwen3/DeepSeek-Qwen/MedReason/MedS3).
The curriculum-ordering ablation (Appendix H) is a valuable sanity check that isolates the contribution of the high-to-low resource schedule rather than just attributing gains to RL/SFT alone.

Results are internally consistent: gains scale with model size, and the language-consistency/logical-accuracy trade-off improves jointly rather than one at the expense of the other, which is a meaningful finding if the underlying evaluation is trustworthy.
Reasonable documentation of training hyperparameters, prompts, and reward design in the appendix, aiding partial reproducibility for the parts that don't depend on closed APIs.
weaknesses: Severe evaluation circularity: the benchmark is constructed by prompting GPT-4o to generate content, correctness reward during RL uses GPT-4.1 as verifier, and final evaluation again uses GPT-4o as judge. This means reported 'logical correctness' gains largely measure alignment with GPT-4-family outputs/preferences rather than independently validated clinical ground truth, undermining the central claim that CURE-MED improves genuine medical reasoning.

Questionable data provenance for low-resource languages: MedlinePlus is predominantly English-language, yet the paper claims GPT-4o 'queries MedlinePlus content and drafts... questions' natively and independently in Amharic, Yoruba, Hausa, Swahili, etc.; it is unclear how clinically grounded and linguistically natural such generations can be for languages where GPT-4o has limited native proficiency, casting doubt on the claimed clinical validity of the 'ground truth'.

Human verification results appear implausibly high and under-specified: many languages report exact 5.00/5 scores in both clinical correctness and language quality, with no reported number of raters per language, inter-rater agreement, or rejection/revision rates, weakening confidence that this validation was rigorous rather than a superficial pass/fail check.

Reproducibility is significantly limited by heavy dependence on proprietary APIs (GPT-4o, GPT-4.1) for data generation, reward computation, and evaluation at every stage; the paper acknowledges this as a limitation but does not provide open alternatives, making independent verification of results costly and potentially infeasible for many researchers.

The composite reward weighting (0.65/0.30/0.05) and other design choices (retention ratio α=0.85, tier assignments) are not ablated or well justified beyond the single reported configuration, so sensitivity of results to these hyperparameters is unknown.

Reported improvements are extremely large in places (e.g., 40-80 percentage-point jumps for naive vs. code-switched SFT, near-perfect scores for 32B models), which combined with the judge circularity concern raises the possibility that part of the measured gain reflects better adherence to the reward model's/judge's stylistic preferences (e.g., structured tags) rather than purely improved clinical reasoning.

No statistical significance testing is reported beyond mean ± std over three runs; given the reliance on a single stochastic LLM judge, more rigorous uncertainty quantification (e.g., across multiple judges or human spot-checks correlated with automatic scores) would strengthen soundness claims.
Minor writing/formatting issues (e.g., capitalization inconsistencies, dense related-work citation lists) suggest the paper could benefit from an additional editing pass.
